subject: Dedicated capacity: queueing carveout and throughput guarantees for ACME AI

Subject: Dedicated capacity: queueing carveout & throughput guarantees

Hi Soojin,

We need to align on behavior for our Dedicated pool. Over the past month we saw two incidents where a scheduled nightly batch job bumped up queueing on our reserved GPUs and caused p99 latency for our customer-facing endpoints to jump from ~120ms to ~420ms for ~10 minutes. Our SLAs with end-customers require <200ms p99.

Can Redwood provide a carveout or hard isolation for latency-sensitive routes? Options we want to explore:
- Reserve a small subset of GPUs exclusively for priority inference (no spillover)
- A priority queue that prevents batch work from impacting latency when queue depth > X
- Pre-agreed fallback to a lighter model variant if queueing spike persists, plus clear triggers

We'd like to understand feasibility, the impact on throughput guarantees (tokens/sec) for our bulk jobs, and whether this requires an SLA amendment / credits. Attaching a short summary of the incident (ops attached logs).

Thanks,
Samantha
Samantha Green
Head of Platform Engineering, ACME AI

Hi Samantha — thanks for the details and the logs. We definitely want to avoid those spikes affecting customer-facing latency. A few clarifying Qs before Rishi and I size options:
- Which endpoints must keep p99 < 200ms (list of routes or tags)?
- Typical token/sec for priority traffic during peak (avg and 95th)?
- Nightly batch profile: concurrent requests, tokens per request, and window duration.

From a product/ops perspective we commonly propose three paths (short descriptions below) — we'll sketch tradeoffs once we have your numbers:
1) Hard carveout: reserve N GPUs for priority endpoints only (no batching for background jobs). Predictable latency but reduces shared capacity for bulk jobs.
2) Priority lanes + queue caps: keep resources shared but enforce a fast-path priority queue. When priority queue length > threshold, background requests are throttled or deferred. Better utilization, more complexity.
3) Model-fallback SLO: allow background jobs to use reserved pool but with an automatic fallback to a smaller model variant for overflow. This preserves throughput for bulk but changes output quality.

I'll loop in Rishi for the queueing mechanics and Laura for commercial terms. If you can share the traffic metrics above I'll put together simulated impacts and a proposed SLA amendment.

Best,
Soojin Lee
Account Executive, Redwood Inference

Hi all — quick technical write-up on how Dedicated pool queueing behaves and what we can change: 

Current behavior (short):
- Dedicated pools are a set of pinned GPU nodes. By default we use workload-aware continuous batching and a shared request queue per node group.
- Each GPU has a concurrency slot model: up to M concurrent streams depending on model size (for your Llama-70B variant M ~= 4). When queue backs up, batching increases batch size which reduces per-token cost but increases latency for tail requests.

Options we can implement and tradeoffs: 
A) Hard carveout (recommended for strict p99 targets): reserve 4 GPUs for priority routes. These GPUs will never be filled by batch jobs. Result: predictable p99, but your batch throughput will drop by the reserved capacity (can be made up with short-term burst capacity into a shared burst pool if purchased).

B) Priority lane + queue caps: implement a two-queue system — priority queue always takes first pass; background queue is rate-limited when priority queue length > L. Pros: high utilization, no hard capacity loss. Cons: complexity in enforcement and slightly higher operational overhead; under extreme load background jobs can be deferred or delayed. We can set L=8 as starting point per node group.

C) Model fallback & graceful degradation: configure automatic fallback to a quantized variant (e.g., 8-bit quant) or a smaller model when a per-request wait exceeds T ms. This keeps throughput but changes output quality; good for non-critical batch work.

Measurement & SLA mechanics:
- We can define priority endpoints and attach SLOs (p50/p95/p99) measured on the priority carved GPUs.
- Credits: standard formula we use is pro-rated uptime / 30-day window with thresholds (example: p99 <= 150ms for a month -> no credits; p99 150-250ms -> 5% monthly usage credit; >250ms -> 15% credit). We can adjust.

Next steps from my side: I'll run a short sim (queueing-sim-results.csv) for your nightly batch profile if you share the tokens/sec and concurrency. Also list which routes must be prioritized.

Thanks,
Rishi Malhotra
Senior Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference

Thanks Rishi — helpful breakdown. Quick answers:
- Priority endpoints: /inference/realtime/* and /chat/* (these comprise ~65% of revenue-sensitive calls)
- Priority traffic at peak: 850 req/s, average 22 tokens/request, 95th token/sec ~ 20k tokens/s
- Nightly batch: peak window 02:00-03:30 PST, ~600 concurrent jobs, avg 1200 tokens/job

We prefer option A (hard carveout) if we can get a clear p99 guarantee for the priority GPUs and reasonable commercial offset for the lost batch throughput. We're OK with fallback for low-priority background jobs.

Also — what's the lead time to implement carveout + the SLA amendment? Procurement wants to know if this affects contract start date.

Samantha

Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity: queueing carveout & throughput guarantees

Hi Samantha — following up with commercial terms based on the carveout ask. Attached is a formal proposal (SLA_proposal_ACME_v2.pdf). Summary here: 
- Proposed carveout: 4 dedicated GPUs reserved for priority endpoints (no background jobs).
- Burst: 10% burst capacity into shared pool for short spikes (subject to available capacity).
- SLA: p99 latency target for priority endpoints measured on reserved GPUs = 150ms (30-day rolling window).
- Credits: 5% monthly usage credit if p99 between 150-250ms; 15% if >250ms for the month. Credits apply to Hosted usage charges only; Dedicated reservation fee unaffected.
- Implementation lead time: 14 business days after signature for carveout + monitoring hooks; SLA amendment executed concurrently via DocuSign.

If ACME needs a different credit formula or a longer lead time for rollout we can negotiate. Once we have sign-off I will create an implementation playbook and schedule a joint runbook/test in staging.

Best,
Laura Bennett
Sr. Customer Success Manager, Redwood Inference
